The reproductive biology of the Portuguese sole, Dagetichthys lusitanicus, has been the subject of several detailed field investigations along the Iberian Atlantic coast. Females attain a maximum recorded total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger pleuronectiforms in their estuarine and coastal habitats. The fertilised eggs of this species are demersal and adhesive, each possessing a diameter of approximately 0.7 millimeters, which yields a remarkably small calculated wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minimal neonatal mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva during the brief period before the onset of exogenous feeding. Field surveys indicate that adult females, after reaching asymptotic size, commonly attain a maximum wet weight of 810 grams [Wwi = 810 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions calibrated on local population samples. Such a substantial increase from the larval stage underscores the rapid growth trajectory characteristic of this flatfish during its first year of benthic life.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 26.6 °C [T = 26.6 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for the Portuguese sole has been documented at 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days]. At this same thermal regime, the maximum reproductive rate observed in gravid females attained an impressive annual output. A female producing roughly 300,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 300,000 eggs per spawning event] and completing a single such event each year [F_R_i = single such event each year] approaches the highest fecundity documented for a soleid of this body size. The synchrony between gamete release and the thermal optimum at this temperature appears critical for ensuring high fertilisation success in the wild.

The transition from the planktonic larval phase to a benthic juvenile existence represents a critical period in the life cycle of Dagetichthys lusitanicus. Following metamorphic climax and settlement, post-metamorphic juveniles begin the gradual process of sexual maturation. Available growth data indicate that the total length at which puberty is attained in this species is 27.5 centimeters [Lp = 27.5 centimeters], a size corresponding to roughly sixty-nine percent of the ultimate length reached by females. At this approximate length, the predicted wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 140 grams [Wwp = 140 grams], based on the same length-weight relationship applied to the adult population. Individuals at this stage exhibit the beginnings of gonadal recrudescence, marking the transition from an immature sub-adult to a reproductively viable organism. The attainment of this size threshold is typically reached during the second or third year of life, depending on local productivity conditions.

Comparative analysis with other soleid species from the northeastern Atlantic reveals several distinctive life-history features in Dagetichthys lusitanicus. The ultimate total length for females of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] is somewhat smaller than that reported for the common sole, Solea solea, which can exceed 50 centimeters, but it is consistent with the size range observed in congeneric species such as Dagetichthys marginatus. Similarly, the ultimate wet weight of 810 grams [Wwi = 810 grams] positions the Portuguese sole as a medium-sized flatfish within its community. Interestingly, the wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] is among the lowest recorded for a soleid, likely an adaptation linked to the production of numerous small pelagic eggs rather than fewer, larger demersal ones. This reproductive strategy prioritises high fecundity over individual offspring provisioning, a trade-off that is energetically favourable in productive estuarine nursery grounds where planktonic food availability for exotrophic larvae is seasonally abundant.

At the optimal temperature of 26.6 °C [T = 26.6 °C], the lifespan of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] is thought to reflect a balance between metabolic acceleration at warmer temperatures and the cumulative costs of repeated reproduction. Field tagging studies have further refined the estimate for the total length at puberty, confirming that most individuals in wild populations commence gametogenesis between 26 and 29 centimeters total length, with the central value of 27.5 centimeters [Lp = 27.5 centimeters] serving as a robust population-level descriptor. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 140 grams [Wwp = 140 grams] aligns well with the general length-weight trend observed in the region. These demographic parameters collectively indicate a life history characterised by moderate longevity, early maturation relative to ultimate size, and a high reproductive output that buffers against the stochastic mortality typical of shallow coastal environments.
